translationRepairs: After Taizu seized the throne, Rong was made prefect of Cao, military commissioner of Zhenning, honorary grand tutor, and associate grand councilor.
After Taizu seized the throne, Rong was made prefect of Chan, military commissioner of Zhenning, honorary grand tutor, and associate grand councilor.

Focus unit appoints Rong 澶州刺史; 澶州 is Chan/Chanzhou, not Cao (曹州). The before text invents the wrong prefecture; the proposed Chan correction matches the Chinese place name and leaves the rest of the offices intact.
On guimao Zheng Renhui was posted to guard the Eastern Capital.
On guiwei Zheng Renhui was posted to guard the Eastern Capital.
Focus unit dates the posting 癸未; 癸未 is guiwei, not guimao (癸卯). Neighboring 辛巳 and 乙酉 confirm the cycle position. The replacement corrects only the sexagenary day.
On guimao Zheng Renhui was left to guard the Eastern Capital.
On guiwei Zheng Renhui was left to guard the Eastern Capital.
Same focus unit reads 癸未 (guiwei). The literal before misreads it as guimao; the proposed guiwei reading matches the Chinese day name.
On guimao Lady Liu of Pengcheng was posthumously enthroned as empress.
On guiwei Lady Liu of Pengcheng was posthumously enthroned as empress.
Focus unit dates the posthumous enthronement 癸未; that is guiwei, not guimao. The replacement fixes only the day name while preserving the rest of the sentence.
On guimao Lady Liu of Pengcheng commandery was posthumously installed as empress.
On guiwei Lady Liu of Pengcheng commandery was posthumously installed as empress.
Same focus unit has 癸未 (guiwei). The literal before wrongly has guimao; the proposed reading is the correct sexagenary transcription.
On guimao Shu sent back Hu Li, Zhou’s prefect of Pu Prefecture.
On guiwei Shu sent back Hu Li, Zhou’s prefect of Pu Prefecture.
Focus unit dates Shu’s return of Hu Li 癸未; 癸未 is guiwei, not guimao. The proposed day correction is accurate and otherwise leaves the sentence unchanged.
On guimao Shu returned Hu Li, our prefect of Pu Prefecture.
On guiwei Shu returned Hu Li, our prefect of Pu Prefecture.
Same focus unit reads 癸未 (guiwei). The literal before misreads the day as guimao; the replacement restores the correct sexagenary name.

Year two opens with Ouyang Xiu’s note: in the Five Dynasties’ chaos five heirs took throne, yet four broke ancient practice on era names. Liang’s last emperor and Jin’s deposed emperor waited more than a year; Han’s Hidden Emperor and Zhou’s Shizong kept prior reign titles for life. The annals do not rebuke them—they record facts, and the fault is plain.

In the second year: in the chaotic age of the Five Dynasties, five successors took the throne, yet four did not change the reign title according to ancient practice. Liang’s last emperor and Jin’s deposed emperor, more than a year after accession, ought to have changed the era name but did not, changing only the following year. Han’s Hidden Emperor and Zhou’s Shizong both kept their predecessors’ era names to the end without change, and the annals offer no censure—they simply record the facts, and the fault shows itself.

Focus unit begins 二年五代乱世… with no authorial frame naming Ouyang Xiu. The before text invents “Ouyang Xiu’s note” and compresses the 逾年…又明年然后改 detail; the proposed wording restores the Chinese comment without the invented attribution.

Cold Food sacrifices in the open with spirit money burned, a new reign title proclaimed amid mourning while music played, Ma Yanji and Ren Yuan put to death—ritual, music, punishments, and policy were all but destroyed.

Cold Food sacrifices in the open with spirit money burned, a new reign title proclaimed amid mourning while music played, Ma Yan and Ren Yuan put to death—ritual, music, punishments, and policy were all but destroyed.
Focus unit has 杀马延及任圜: 马延 is Ma Yan and 及 joins him to 任圜. The before text wrongly folds 及 into the personal name as Yanji; the proposed Ma Yan reading matches the Chinese.
On gengyin younger brothers Xi Rang were enfeoffed as Prince of Cao, Xi Jin as Prince of Ji, and Xi Hui as Prince of Qi.
On gengyin younger brother Xi Rang was enfeoffed as Prince of Cao, Xi Jin as Prince of Ji, and Xi Hui as Prince of Qi.

Focus unit lists three separate enfeoffments beginning 封弟熙让为曹王; Xi Rang is a singular subject of the first clause. The before text’s “younger brothers Xi Rang were” is ungrammatical; the proposed singular wording matches the Chinese structure.
